issues.legal_issue: Administrative minimum-price guidelines cannot displace the registration officer’s independent assessment of whether a property’s value or consideration has been truly stated.
material_facts: Government instructions prescribed floor prices and stated that they were minimum prices to be used as guidelines.
The registration officer considered the declared value inadequate by reference to the instructions and required the instrument to be revised.
The value of property can vary between localities, so a fixed minimum cannot determine the true value in every transaction.
issues.conclusion: The instructions were inconsistent with the governing law insofar as they inhibited the registration officer’s independent, quasi-judicial assessment. Guidelines may serve as prima facie material to alert the officer, but cannot control that assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 47A(1) of the Indian Stamp Act requires the registration officer to form an objective, reasonable belief that the value or consideration has not been truly stated. Government guidelines may provide prima facie material, but the officer must independently assess the value in light of prevailing prices in the relevant locality. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.challenge_to_state_valuation_guidelines: The proceeding challenges government guidance used by registration officers when assessing declared property values.
predicates.guidelines_prescribe_fixed_minimum_value: The government guidance sets floor or minimum prices for property transactions.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges government guidance that sets minimum prices, the guidance may inform, but may not control, the registration officer’s independent value assessment.

issues.legal_issue: A registration officer who suspects that a property-transfer instrument understates value must register it before referring the valuation for determination and cannot withhold registration pending revision.
material_facts: A property-transfer instrument was presented for registration with a declared value lower than the value the registration officer considered applicable.
The registration officer required the parties to revise the instrument before proceeding with registration.
The statutory procedure allowed the officer to refer a suspected undervaluation to the Collector after registering the instrument.
issues.conclusion: The registration officer must register the instrument and, if the officer has reason to believe that the value or consideration has not been truly stated, refer it to the Collector for determination; the officer is not empowered to withhold registration.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 47A(1) of the Indian Stamp Act, the registration officer may refer a potentially undervalued instrument to the Collector only after registering it. Under Sections 47A(2) and (3), the Collector determines value and duty through the prescribed inquiry, and Section 47A(4) provides an appeal to the District Judge. The statutory explanation bases value on the price the property would have fetched in the open market on the date of execution. No earlier cases are cited.

predicates.challenge_to_registration_process: The proceeding challenges how a registration officer handled a presented property-transfer instrument whose declared value was considered inaccurate.
predicates.property_transfer_instrument_presented: A person presented an instrument transferring property to a registration officer for registration.
predicates.registrar_suspects_understatement: The registration officer had reason to believe that the instrument did not truly state the property’s value or the transaction’s consideration.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns a presented property-transfer instrument and the registration officer suspects understatement, the instrument must be registered before the valuation is referred for determination.
